summary.text: A previously well eight-year-old male had a two-week history of gradually worsening right-sided neck pain, initially diagnosed in primary care as a sport-related musculoskeletal injury, then neck spasms treated as torticollis with oral diazepam. On paediatric assessment he was afebrile with neck tenderness and palpable cervical nodes; CRP was 37.4 mg/L and neck ultrasound showed likely reactive bilateral lymphadenopathy. IV ceftriaxone was started.

He re-presented the next day with severe worsening neck pain and fever of 38.4°C and was admitted. An initial blood culture grew a likely contaminant and a repeat was negative. MRI on day 6 and a cervical spine MRI showed C3 and C4 changes indicating osteomyelitis, and treatment was escalated on day 7 to IV meropenem and vancomycin.

Further tests were negative or unremarkable apart from positive EBV IgG: CMV, HIV, TB T-SPOT, lumbar puncture, urine culture, echocardiography and MRSA swabs. ASOT was 400 IU/mL, ESR 77 mm/hr and complement normal; a positive beta-D-glucan was judged a meropenem-related false positive. Dental caries were found but considered an unlikely source.

After clinical improvement the antibiotics were stepped down on day 25, but fever spikes recurred and CRP rose from 17.7 to 213.3 mg/L, so the MDT re-escalated to IV vancomycin and meropenem with improvement. Repeat imaging showed no collection, so aspiration or surgery was not warranted. Vancomycin was changed to teicoplanin on day 36 and meropenem to ertapenem; MRI on day 70 showed regression, and IV antibiotics were extended, interrupted by line problems.

The total intravenous antibiotic course lasted approximately 16 weeks; after six weeks of admission he moved to the paediatric virtual ward for home IV therapy. MRI four months after admission confirmed full resolution, and follow-up at seven months confirmed full recovery with no persistent neck pain or residual complications, with a normal neurological examination throughout.

ambiguities.issue: The sentence reporting the additional tests states that CMV, HIV, EBV, random blood glucose and TB T-SPOT tests were negative except for positive EBV IgG. Which other EBV markers were tested is not stated, and a negative result for a random blood glucose is unusual wording.

evidence.quote: Additional tests, including cytomegalovirus (CMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), random blood glucose, and tuberculosis (TB) (T-SPOT) tests, were negative, except for positive EBV IgG

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not infer other EBV markers, a numeric glucose value, or that the glucose result was abnormal.

ambiguities.issue: The case text gives bare day numbers (day 4, 6, 7, 25, 36, 70) without naming their origin, and one as "day 5 of admission". The bare day numbers are read as one narrative count and order each other; day 5 of admission is not ordered against them because admission was the day after presentation and the origin of the bare count is not stated.

evidence.quote: On day 4, following microbiology consultant advice, IV metronidazole was added to the antimicrobial regimen.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not convert day numbers to calendar dates or offsets, and do not order day 5 of admission against the bare day numbers.
